```{r setup}
suppressPackageStartupMessages({library(tidyverse); library(knitr)})
options(knitr.kable.NA = "n/a")
P <- normalizePath("..")
tab <- function(f) read_csv(file.path(P, "output/tables", f), show_col_types = FALSE)
# Review-2 tables carry LB06 codes ("01", "03", "10") that must stay character.
tabc <- function(f) read_csv(file.path(P, "output/tables", f), show_col_types = FALSE,
                             col_types = cols(.default = col_guess(), g1 = col_character(),
                                              g2 = col_character(), group = col_character()))
der <- function(f) read_csv(file.path(P, "data/derived", f), show_col_types = FALSE)
# Relative, not absolute: Quarto resolves figure paths against the qmd
# directory and prefixes "./", which breaks an absolute path.
fig <- function(f) file.path("..", "output/figures", f)
verd  <- tab("t27_basket_verdicts.csv")
cumg  <- tab("t28_cumulative_gaps.csv")
dimv  <- tab("t30_dimension_verdicts.csv")
rob   <- tab("t31_robustness.csv")
burd  <- tab("t24_burden_by_group.csv")
nec   <- tab("t25_necessity_shares.csv")
fdef  <- tabc("t37_family_definitions.csv")
comp  <- tabc("t38_comparators.csv")
wtim  <- tabc("t39_weight_timing.csv")
wint  <- tabc("t41_window_tests.csv")
rcpi  <- tab("t45_rcpi_i_benchmark.csv")
BLAB <- c(pm_oer_all_in = "CPI concept, medical pooled (headline)",
          oer_all_in = "CPI concept, medical unpooled",
          pm_ex_shelter = "Ex-shelter, medical pooled",
          pm_all_in = "All-in without owner shelter, medical pooled",
          all_in = "All-in without owner shelter",
          ex_shelter = "Ex-shelter", ex_housing = "Ex-housing",
          all_in_long = "All-in, long panel", ex_shelter_long = "Ex-shelter, long panel")
GL <- c("01" = "All consumer units", "03" = "Married couples without children",
        "04" = "Married couples with children, any age (04)",
        "05" = "Married, oldest child under 6 (05)", "06" = "Married, oldest child 6 to 17 (06)",
        "07" = "Married, oldest child 18 or older (07)", "09" = "One parent, child under 18 (09)",
        "10" = "Single-person and other consumer units",
        F1 = "Families with children, headline (04 + 09)",
        K1 = "Families with a child under 18 (05 + 06 + 09)",
        RF = "All other consumer units")
pfmt <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p))
```

## Abstract {.unnumbered}

Households with children buy a different basket of goods than other
households, and item-level inflation rates diverge. That raises an obvious
question: do families experience higher inflation than the headline CPI
implies? This paper builds group-specific price indices from Consumer
Expenditure Survey budget shares and CPI-U item indices, pricing owner housing
with owners' equivalent rent weighted by the same CE rental-value question BLS
uses. **Families did not face higher inflation.** Between December 2019 and
July 2026 prices rose 29.4 percent for families with children and 30.1
percent for single-person and other consumer units, a gap of $-0.7$
percentage points, about 0.1 point a year. The gap exceeds CE sampling error
if errors are independent across survey years but not under the worst-case
correlation, and it shrinks to about $-0.5$ on a superlative index with
contemporaneous weights. Its sign depends on the comparison: families' prices
rose 0.2 points less than all households' and 0.2 points more than those of
married couples without children, neither distinguishable from zero. The
robust finding is that household type barely moves inflation.

The differences that exist follow housing's share of the budget, not
children. Single households devote 36 percent of the basket to shelter
against 30 percent for families, and shelter rose 33.5 percent against 27.9
percent for everything else. Childcare, the most family-specific category,
contributes nothing, because its price rose at the average rate. The 12-month
gap turned briefly positive in 2021-22, but over those two years it cumulated
to $+0.2$ points, not distinguishable from zero, and it reversed in 2023-24.
The same machinery finds an income gradient about three times larger and of
opposite sign, close to what BLS's own research index by income quintile
shows for the same period.

Rates are not burdens. The same inflation cost married-couple families about
\$16,300 a year in non-housing spending, against about \$8,100 for
single-person households.

## The question, and why the answer is not obvious

Headline CPI-U describes a single average urban household. Real households buy
different baskets, and if families with children concentrate their spending in
categories whose prices rose fastest, their true cost of living rose faster than
the published index implies. This is the *composition channel*, and it is the
mechanism behind BLS's own experimental index for the elderly and behind the
academic literature on inflation inequality [@hobijn2005; @jaravel2021].

There is a second channel this paper cannot reach. Within a CPI item stratum,
different households pay different prices and face different variety and quality
trajectories. @kaplan2017 find this *price-faced channel* is large at the
household level. Because CPI item indices are common to all households by
construction, everything here is the composition channel alone, and the
price-faced channel could widen the family gap or narrow it.

The sign was not obvious in advance. Families with children are
disproportionately homeowners and single-person households disproportionately
renters. Food away from home skews single; food at home, vehicles and gasoline
skew family. Which effect dominates depends on the window and on how shelter is
treated, which is why the shelter variants below were specified before the
index was estimated. (CPI rent and owners' equivalent rent themselves moved
together: 33.0 and 33.9 percent from December 2019 to July 2026.)

## Data

Both surveys come from the BLS time-series flat files.

**Consumer Expenditure Survey** (prefix `cx`), dimension `LB06`, composition of
consumer unit. Annual mean expenditures per consumer unit, 1988 to 2024. The
headline family group is married couples with children plus one-parent
households with a child under 18, pooled by consumer-unit counts, against
single-person and other consumer units. The CE's married-with-children group
counts children of any age, so it includes couples whose children are all
adults; @sec-whom re-estimates with families that have a child under 18.

**CPI-U** (prefix `cu`), national, not seasonally adjusted, monthly through July
2026. NSA is the right basis because relative importance is published NSA and
seasonal factors are revised annually. CPI-W and seasonally adjusted CPI-U are
used for robustness.

**CE calendar-year workbooks** of means, shares and standard errors,
2012 to 2024. These supply what the flat files lack: standard errors for every
expenditure mean, and the estimated monthly rental value of owned homes by
household type. Parsed means reconcile to the flat files in 3,159 of 3,176
cells exactly, the rest within \$30.

Expenditures are organised into a 41-category taxonomy that partitions total
expenditure. Additivity to the published total is asserted for every year and
group: 201 cells, zero failures, worst discrepancy 0.016 percent.

Three data hazards deserve flagging because each produced a wrong answer before
being caught.

*CEX `display_level` is not a tree.* Household operations does not equal the sum
of its apparent children, because Personal services contains the childcare item
at the same display level. Every aggregate used here is a BLS-published total.

*BLS published no October 2025 CPI.* That month carries 11 series against 380 in
September, and the all-items index itself is absent. The month is excluded from
the price grid rather than interpolated, and the chain is carried across it with
the true September-to-November relative, so index levels remain correct on both
sides. Any analysis assuming contiguous monthly CPI rows will produce wrong
12-month changes for a year afterwards.

*BLS omits the `LB06` all-consumer-units series for 2010 to 2013 entirely.* Those
cells were borrowed from an equivalent dimension after verifying that the two
agree exactly across 10,727 item-year overlaps. This was found only in the index
stage, because an additivity check inspects cells that exist and passes silently
on cells that are absent.

## Method

### The index

A group-specific chained Laspeyres with BLS-style price-updated cost weights.
For month $t$ in calendar year $Y$, with expenditure shares from CEX year
$V = Y-2$ (the CPI convention since the 2023 move to annual weight updates):

$$c_{i,t} = s_{i,V}\,\frac{p_{i,t-1}}{\bar p_{i,V}}, \qquad
w_{i,t} = \frac{c_{i,t}}{\sum_k c_{k,t}}, \qquad
P^g_t = P^g_{t-1}\sum_i w_{i,t}\,\frac{p_{i,t}}{p_{i,t-1}}$$

where $\bar p_{i,V}$ is the category's average price in the expenditure year.
Price updating converts a static expenditure share into the cost weight CPI
uses. Updating only from December $Y-1$, or not at all, moves the headline
cumulative gap by 0.08 points. @sec-formula replaces the lagged Laspeyres with
a superlative index.

Mapping CEX categories to CPI item strata required a hand-built crosswalk, since
BLS publishes no concordance in either flat-file directory. It maps 37 of the 41
categories onto 62 CPI item strata, 12 of them as composites aggregated by
relative importance. For all 25 single-item categories across 8,353 monthly
observations, the chained index reproduces published CPI with a worst absolute
error of 0.00000000.

### Owner housing

CPI prices owner-occupied shelter through rental equivalence, while the CEX
flat files report owner *outlays* (mortgage interest, property taxes,
maintenance). Without an equivalent-rent weight a family index either omits
owners' housing or prices the wrong thing. In the basket without it, families
carry a rent weight of 6.4 percent against 15.8 percent for the comparison group
while almost none of their housing costs appear.

The CE workbooks carry the missing piece: the estimated monthly rental value of
owned homes by household type. That is the survey question BLS uses to weight
owners' equivalent rent in the CPI. The headline basket replaces owner outlays
with twelve times that value, priced by the CPI OER index. The implied
all-households ratio of owner rental value to rent outlays is 2.9 to 3.4 across
2012-2024, against 3.0 to 3.7 for the CPI's own OER-to-rent relative
importance.

### Medical care

The largest remaining disagreement between CEX and CPI weights is medical, with
opposite signs within the block: CEX households report out-of-pocket premiums
as insurance, about eight times CPI's health insurance weight, while CPI routes
most medical spending through services. Priced as is, that places a large
weight on CPI's retained-earnings health insurance index, which fell 19.0
percent from December 2019 to July 2026 while CPI rose 29.9 percent. The
headline pools medical care into one block aggregated with CPI weights.

### Baskets

The headline basket, fixed before the revised estimates were run, is the **CPI
concept**: every mapped category, owners' equivalent rent, medical pooled,
about 98 of 100 CPI relative-importance points, from January 2014. Its
all-households version tracks published CPI-U to a mean absolute 0.10 points on
12-month changes. The co-headline removes shelter entirely. Seven other
baskets are reported to show the range.

### Two yardsticks

**Sampling error.** CE standard errors are propagated to the gap by the delta
method. With group inflation $\pi_g = \sum_i w_i r_i$ and $w_i \propto x_i u_i$,
$\partial \pi_g / \partial \log x_i = w_i (r_i - \pi_g)$, and a common scale
component of sampling error cancels exactly because
$\sum_i w_i (r_i - \pi_g) = 0$. Every CE household-type group is a
consumer-unit-weighted mix of seven disjoint published cells, so the
derivatives are taken with respect to each cell's category means. That gets
the covariance right when the two groups overlap, as families and all
households do. Category means are treated as uncorrelated within a cell. Two
conventions for correlation across survey years are reported: independent,
and the worst case over any correlation, which adds the standard deviations of
the annual links. The truth lies between, because CE interview households stay
in the sample for about a year and adjacent survey years share respondents.

**Weight-source discrepancy.** The all-households index rebuilt with CPI's
published relative importance instead of CEX shares, same basket, formula and
prices. This bounds how much the weight *concept* moves index levels. Most of it
is common to every CEX group and differences out of a gap, so it is reported
alongside, not used as a test.

## Results

### Families did not face higher inflation than single households

```{r headline}
cumg |>
  filter(pair == "fam", from == as.Date("2019-12-01")) |>
  left_join(filter(verd, pair == "fam") |> select(basket, mean_gap), by = "basket") |>
  transmute(Basket = BLAB[basket], `Families (%)` = cum_1, `Single/other (%)` = cum_2,
            `Gap (pp)` = gap_pp, `95% CI, independent` = 1.96 * se_indep,
            `95% CI, worst case` = 1.96 * se_corr, `Mean 12m gap` = mean_gap) |>
  arrange(match(Basket, BLAB)) |>
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Cumulative price change December 2019 to July 2026, families with children and single-person and other consumer units, every basket. Confidence intervals from CE sampling error with errors independent across survey years and in the worst case.")
```

On the headline basket prices rose 29.42 percent for families with children and
30.11 percent for single-person and other consumer units. The gap of $-0.69$
points is small, about 0.1 point a year. Measured against CE sampling error it
is 3.7 standard errors if errors are independent across survey years, and 1.6
in the worst case ($p = 0.11$). Every basket that avoids the health-insurance
problem below puts families 0.4 to 1.0 points below single households. Those
baskets share the same survey samples, so that is robustness to specification,
not to sampling.

The two baskets near zero, ex-shelter and ex-housing without pooling, are the
ones that price CEX health insurance with CPI's retained-earnings index. That
single series also pulls their levels about five points below published CPI.
An earlier version of this paper headlined the ex-shelter basket (25.3 against
25.3 percent) and judged the gap against a yardstick that covered only
2013-2020. Both choices are corrected here.

![The twelve-month family gap with its 95 percent sampling interval.](`r fig("f09_gap_vs_errorbar.png")`){#fig-gap}

### Compared with whom, and which families? {#sec-whom}

The headline compares families with a residual category that pools single
people, roommates, the young and the elderly. Changing the comparison changes
the sign.

```{r comparators}
comp |>
  filter(variant == "headline", g1 == "F1") |>
  select(basket, g2, gap, p_indep, p_bound) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = basket, values_from = c(gap, p_indep, p_bound)) |>
  transmute(`Families with children minus` = GL[g2],
            `Gap, CPI concept (pp)` = gap_oer,
            `p, independent / worst case` = paste(pfmt(p_indep_oer), "/", pfmt(p_bound_oer)),
            `Gap, ex-shelter (pp)` = gap_exsh,
            `p, ex-shelter` = paste(pfmt(p_indep_exsh), "/", pfmt(p_bound_exsh))) |>
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Headline families against four comparison groups, cumulative December 2019 to July 2026. All other consumer units is everyone outside the headline family group.")
```

Against all households, families' prices rose 0.20 points less; against
married couples without children, 0.20 points more. Neither is
distinguishable from zero. On the non-housing basket, families ran 0.89 points
above childless couples ($p = 0.001$ with independent errors, $0.16$ in the
worst case). Two lifecycle categories drive the comparison with childless
couples and nearly cancel on the full basket. Childless couples, whose
reference person averages 60 years old, carry more medical weight, and
medical prices rose slowly; that adds 0.36 points to families' relative
inflation. They also carry more owners'-equivalent-rent weight, and OER rose
fast; that subtracts 0.36. The ordering of groups tracks age and household
size, through shelter and medical care, more than children.

```{r definitions}
fdef |>
  filter(g2 == "10") |>
  select(basket, g1, gap, se_indep, se_bound) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = basket, values_from = c(gap, se_indep, se_bound)) |>
  transmute(`Group minus single/other` = GL[g1], `Gap, CPI concept (pp)` = gap_oer,
            `SE, independent` = se_indep_oer, `SE, worst case` = se_bound_oer,
            `Gap, ex-shelter (pp)` = gap_exsh) |>
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Family definitions, each minus single-person and other consumer units, cumulative December 2019 to July 2026.")
```

The CE's married-with-children group includes couples whose children are all
adults, who spend \$129 a year on childcare. Restricting to families with a
child under 18 widens the gap to $-0.84$ points, so the headline is, if
anything, conservative. Within families the differences are larger than
between families and anyone else: married couples whose oldest child is 6 to
17 are furthest below single households ($-1.17$), and one-parent households
are not below them at all ($+0.14$).

![Cumulative gaps for every comparison group and family definition, with 95 percent sampling intervals.](`r fig("f19_definitions_comparators.png")`){#fig-whom}

### Where the gap comes from

Because both groups' weights sum to one, the gap can be written
$\sum_i (w^F_i - w^N_i)(\pi_i - \bar\pi)$ for any $\bar\pi$. Centering on the
all-households change is the only version that attributes it sensibly: a
category matters when families over- or under-weight it *and* its price moved
differently from the average. Without the centering, every category families
over-weight looks like a positive contribution merely because prices rose.

On that basis the December 2019 to July 2026 gap splits roughly in half.
Housing is one half. Single-person and other households put 35.9 percent of
spending into shelter against 29.6 percent for families; the owners'
equivalent rent weights are almost the same (22.1 and 22.7 percent), so the
difference is rent, 12.7 against 5.3. Rent contributes $-0.26$ points
($\pm 0.04$ at 95 percent, independent errors). The other half is the
non-housing mix: education $-0.18$ ($\pm 0.05$), recreation goods $-0.10$,
tobacco $-0.09$ and electricity $-0.07$, against gasoline $+0.18$
($\pm 0.10$). Vehicle purchases carry large CE sampling error ($-0.08 \pm
0.28$), so no vehicle attribution is supported in either direction.

The education term is mostly parents of college-age children. It is $-0.27$
for couples whose oldest child is 18 or older and $-0.13$ for families with a
child under 18. Priced by level, with K-12 tuition on its own CPI series
rather than a composite dominated by college tuition, the under-18 term is
$-0.01$. For families with a child under 18, the non-housing tilt that
lowers their inflation is apparel ($-0.13$), utilities ($-0.07$) and tobacco
($-0.07$).

Childcare is the instructive case. On the CE's childcare items, families carry
about eight times the weight single households do, 1.6 percent of the basket
against 0.2 (twelve times for families with a child under 18), yet childcare
contributes nothing: CPI day care and preschool rose 29.8 percent against 29.9
for all items. Day care has tracked services generally since 2010 (2.6 percent
a year in the 2010s against 2.6 for all services). The childcare problem
families describe is real, and it is the size of the bill: married couples
whose oldest child is under 6 average \$5,586 a year, 6.4 percent of spending,
and that average includes families who pay nothing.

The same forces operate in ordinary years. From December 2014 to December 2019
the gap was $-1.05$ points, clearly outside sampling error: rent $-0.68$ (rent
rose 19.9 percent against 9.1 overall), vehicles and gas $-0.22$ as car prices
fell, childcare $+0.07$. Housing has economies of scale, which is why the
shares differ: it takes 40 percent of a one-person household's spending and 31
percent of a four-person household's.

![Mean contribution to the twelve-month gap by category, 2020 to 2026.](`r fig("f11_gap_contributions.png")`){#fig-contrib}

### The 2021-22 episode, tested once

```{r windows}
wint |>
  filter(variant == "headline", basket == "oer", g1 == "F1", g2 == "10") |>
  transmute(Window = paste(format(from, "%b %Y"), "to", format(to, "%b %Y")),
            `Gap (pp)` = gap, `SE, independent` = se_indep, `SE, worst case` = se_bound,
            `p, independent` = pfmt(p_indep), `p, worst case` = pfmt(p_bound)) |>
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "One test per window: cumulative gap, families with children minus single-person and other consumer units, headline basket.")
```

The 12-month gap was positive from April 2021 to August 2022, peaking at
$+0.60$. A run of positive 12-month readings overstates the evidence, because
overlapping 12-month windows share most of their data. Tested once over the
window, December 2020 to December 2022, families' prices rose 0.23 points
more, which is not distinguishable from zero ($p = 0.13$ with independent
errors). The one precisely estimated piece is rent ($+0.12$), which lagged
other prices while single households carry more of it. Vehicles and gasoline
contribute as much ($+0.19$) but with a 95 percent interval of $\pm 0.25$.
The reversal is not in doubt: from December 2022 to December 2024 families ran
0.65 points below single households, significant under either convention,
led by rent ($-0.36$). Since December 2024 the gap is zero.

### How much the answer depends on the index formula {#sec-formula}

The headline follows CPI practice: two-year-old CE weights, price-updated, in
a Laspeyres formula. The lag is a production constraint that a retrospective
study does not need, and it prices 2022 and 2023 with pandemic-era 2020 and
2021 spending. A Törnqvist index on adjacent CE years' expenditure shares,
the superlative concept behind the C-CPI-U, removes both the lag and the
fixed-basket formula.

```{r formula}
MLAB <- c(lasp_lag2 = "Laspeyres, 2-year-old weights (headline)",
          lasp_lag1 = "Laspeyres, 1-year-old weights",
          lasp_lag0 = "Laspeyres, same-year weights",
          tornqvist = "Tornqvist, adjacent CE years")
wtim |>
  filter(variant == "headline", basket == "oer", method %in% names(MLAB),
         from %in% as.Date(c("2014-12-01", "2019-12-01")), to %in% as.Date(c("2019-12-01", "2024-12-01"))) |>
  select(method, from, to, group, cum) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = cum) |>
  transmute(Window = paste(format(from, "%b %Y"), "to", format(to, "%b %Y")),
            Method = MLAB[method], `All CUs (%)` = `01`,
            `Families minus single/other` = F1 - `10`, `Families minus all CUs` = F1 - `01`,
            `Families minus childless couples` = F1 - `03`) |>
  arrange(Window, match(Method, MLAB)) |>
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Cumulative gaps (pp) under four weight and formula choices, headline basket. Contemporaneous weights end with the 2024 CE.")
```

Over December 2019 to December 2024 the family-minus-single gap is $-0.47$ on
the Törnqvist against $-0.67$ on the headline formula, and $-0.47$ against
$-0.69$ extended to July 2026. The sign holds and the magnitude falls by about
a third. Against married couples without children, families move to $+0.36$.
Before 2020 the formula barely matters ($-0.99$ against $-1.05$). Most of the
difference sits in the 2023 link, which the headline prices with 2021 CE
weights; the shelter-weight gap between the groups is 6.2 to 6.7 points under
every method, so fresher weights shrink the gap through other categories. For
all households the Törnqvist runs 0.41 points below the Laspeyres over
2019-2024, the same sign as BLS's C-CPI-U minus CPI-U ($-1.35$) and smaller,
as it should be when substitution is measured across 34 categories rather than
BLS's roughly 7,800 item-area cells.

### Other robustness

```{r robust}
rob |>
  filter(pair == "fam", basket %in% c("pm_oer_all_in", "pm_ex_shelter")) |>
  transmute(`Price input` = recode(price_input, cpiu_nsa = "CPI-U, NSA", cpiw_nsa = "CPI-W, NSA",
                                   cpiu_sa = "CPI-U, seasonally adjusted"),
            Basket = BLAB[basket], `Families (%)` = cum_1, `Single/other (%)` = cum_2,
            `Gap (pp)` = cum_gap) |>
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "The headline gap under alternative price inputs, December 2019 to July 2026.")
```

The result does not depend on the price input or the price-updating
convention. Married couples with children alone show $-0.79$ points, and a
size cut, four-person minus one-person consumer units, shows $-0.41$ (not
significant). Splitting five categories into their published sub-items (new
and used vehicles; vehicle insurance, repair and leasing; tuition by level;
childcare separately from elder care) moves the gap to $-0.66$. Removing
vehicle and other finance charges, which CPI excludes as interest, moves it by
0.02 to 0.04 points.

### Family status against income and tenure

A family gap is easier to judge next to gaps the literature expects. The
identical machinery was run on income and tenure.

```{r dimcmp}
dimv |>
  filter(basket == "pm_oer_all_in") |>
  transmute(Cut = gap_label, `Cumulative gap (pp)` = cum_gap,
            `95% CI, independent` = ci95_indep, `95% CI, worst case` = ci95_corr,
            `Mean 12m gap` = mean_gap, `Mean SE` = mean_se) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(`Mean 12m gap`))) |>
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Every cut on the headline basket, December 2019 to July 2026. Renters minus homeowners has no cumulative figure: the CE tenure workbooks start in 2019, so its headline index starts in 2021.")
```

The income gradient is about three times the family gap and runs the other
way. The lowest income quintile faced 1.84 points more cumulative inflation
than the highest, and the lowest decile 2.06 points more. It is led by rent,
with vehicle purchases, which higher-income households buy more of and whose
prices lagged, about as large, though vehicle purchases carry large CE
sampling error. The direction matches the
literature [@jaravel2021; @argente2021].

BLS publishes its own research index by income quintile, built from CE
microdata with households ranked by income adjusted for household size
[@klick2024]. It is the closest external check this method has.

```{r rcpi}
rcpi |>
  filter(kind == "cumulative") |>
  transmute(Window = paste(format(from, "%b %Y"), "to", format(to, "%b %Y")),
            `BLS R-CPI-I` = bls_rcpi_i, `This paper` = ours_laspeyres,
            `BLS R-C-CPI-I (chained)` = bls_r_c_cpi_i, `This paper, Tornqvist` = ours_tornqvist) |>
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Lowest minus highest income quintile, cumulative gap (pp). BLS ranks households by equivalized income; this paper uses the CE's before-tax income quintiles.")
```

Over December 2019 to December 2025 the BLS gap is $+2.15$ points against
$+1.84$ here. The two agree less well before 2020 ($+0.28$ against $+1.27$)
and year by year (correlation 0.47). The income ranking differs: adjusting for
household size moves single-person households up the distribution, and this
paper's lowest quintile carries about twice BLS's excess shelter weight. The
post-2019 agreement is the one to rely on.

![Lowest minus highest income quintile, December-to-December, against BLS's research index.](`r fig("f20_rcpi_i_benchmark.png")`){#fig-rcpi}

Tenure, by contrast, nearly disappears once owners are priced with rental
equivalence: renters minus homeowners averages $+0.03$ points on the 12-month
gap since 2021. The large tenure gap in the basket without owner shelter,
$+4.3$ points since December 2019, is what omitting owners' housing produces.

![Cumulative gaps since December 2019 for every cut.](`r fig("f12_dimension_gaps.png")`){#fig-cuts}

![Cumulative inflation by income quintile, headline basket.](`r fig("f13_income_gradient.png")`){#fig-income}

## Rates are not burdens

The index answers a question about rates. It says nothing about hardship.

```{r burden}
burd |>
  filter(!(dim == "LB06" & code == "01")) |>
  transmute(Group = label, `Inflation, CPI concept (%)` = cum_cpi,
            `Inflation, ex-shelter (%)` = cum_nonshelter,
            `Extra non-shelter cost (USD/yr)` = round(dollars_nonshelter),
            `Extra cost per equivalent adult (USD)` = round(per_equiv_adult),
            `Necessity share (%)` = nec$with_shelter[match(label, nec$label)]) |>
  arrange(desc(`Extra non-shelter cost (USD/yr)`)) |>
  kable(digits = c(0,2,2,0,0,1), format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
        caption = "Cost of buying the 2019 non-shelter basket at July 2026 prices, using each group's own ex-shelter, medical-pooled index. Per equivalent adult divides by the square root of household size. Necessity share is food at home, utilities, rent and owner shelter outlays as a share of 2024 consumption. Tenure groups have no CPI-concept index from December 2019.")
```

Three facts follow.

**Similar rates, unequal dollars.** Married-couple families with children
faced slightly lower inflation than single-person households, and it still
cost them about \$16,300 a year in non-housing spending against about \$8,100.

**Per equivalent adult, families spend more.** Married-couple families spent
\$44,950 per equivalent adult in 2019 against \$35,231 for single-person and
other consumer units, 28 percent more. (Per capita the ranking reverses, but
per-capita comparisons ignore economies of scale.)

**"Families" is not one group.** One-parent households faced 0.92 points more
cumulative inflation than married-couple families on the headline basket
($p = 0.02$ with independent errors, $0.29$ in the worst case). Baskets that
price health insurance with the CPI's retained-earnings index put the gap as
high as 2.9 points, because one-parent households carry the smallest health
insurance share. They devote 43.0 percent of consumption to food at home,
utilities and shelter against 36.6 percent for married-couple families.
Pooling the two, as the headline family index does, averages over this.

![Inflation rates, dollar costs and necessity shares by household type.](`r fig("f14_burden.png")`){#fig-burden}

One number must not be quoted. CEX reported expenditure for the lowest income
quintile is 2.38 times its reported income, a long-documented artifact of income
under-reporting, dissaving, in-kind transfers, and students and retirees drawing
down assets. Any "share of income" figure for that group is meaningless. Use
dollars and necessity shares instead.

## Limitations

1. **The composition channel only.** CPI item indices are common to all
   households, so the price-faced channel of @kaplan2017 is unreachable, and
   it could move the family gap in either direction.
2. **Sampling error is approximate.** The delta method treats category means as
   uncorrelated within a CE cell and ignores CE non-sampling error, notably
   under-reporting. Sub-items without a published standard error borrow their
   parent's.
3. **Owners' equivalent rent rests on self-reported rental value**, as the
   CPI's own OER weight does, and is available only from 2012.
4. **Age is not controlled in the index.** Families with children average 44.3
   years of reference-person age against 53.1 for the comparison group. A
   separate exercise using the CEX age-bracket gradient shows age composition
   runs *against* the rent gap rather than explaining it: renting falls
   steeply with age and families are younger, so age predicts families should
   spend more of their budget on rent, and they spend 10.1 points less. The
   comparison with childless couples in @sec-whom shows age working through
   medical care in the other direction. The flat files publish no cross-tabs,
   so the index itself is unconditional.
5. **Comparison-group composition.** The single-person-and-other category pools
   genuine single-person households with unrelated-adult households, and pools
   the young with the elderly.
6. **Group weights describe a group's aggregate spending**, which gives
   high-spending households more weight than the typical household in the
   group.
7. **Not run:** the full item-level crosswalk, and an age-conditioned or
   household-weighted comparison, both of which require CE microdata.

## Conclusion

Families with children did not face higher inflation than single-person
households over 2019 to 2026. On the index closest to the CPI's own concept
they faced slightly less, about 0.7 points over six and a half years, and
about 0.5 on a superlative index, because single households spend more of
their budget on housing in a period when housing rose fastest. Against all
households or childless couples the difference is a few tenths of a point
either way and not distinguishable from zero. Household type barely moves
inflation. The 2021-22 stretch when families looked worse off is not
distinguishable from zero either, and it reversed.

The comparison that matters more is income. On identical machinery the lowest
income quintile faced 1.8 points more inflation than the highest, close to what
BLS's own research index shows over the same years, led by rent. The
households that need attention are identified by income, by housing exposure,
and by the share of the budget that goes to necessities, where one-parent
households look more like the bottom of the income distribution than like
married-couple families.
